document.title: Deputy Secretary Armitage's Meeting with General Mahmud: Actions and Support Expected of Pakistan in Fight Against Terrorism (State 158711)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
document.note: [Secret] On September 13, 2001 Armitage meets ISI chief Mahmoud Ahmed and presents seven demands for Musharraf's approval. They include stopping al-Qaida at the border, blanket overflight and landing rights, territorial access, intelligence sharing, public condemnation of terrorism, cutting off fuel and recruits to the Taliban, and breaking relations with the Taliban if the evidence implicates bin Ladin.

events.description: Armitage met ISI DG Mahmud Ahmed and delivered a nonpaper listing demands on Pakistan after 9/11.
Armitage's earlier message to Mahmud (REF A).
Terrorist attacks on the US referenced as 'Tuesday's attacks'.
Terrorist attacks on the United States, referred to as 'Tuesday's attacks' and 'September 11'.
Armitage delivered an earlier message to Mahmud the previous day (REF A).

Armitage met ISI DG Mahmud Ahmed, delivering a nonpaper of demands: stop al-Qaida at the border, overflight and landing rights, intelligence sharing, cut fuel to Taliban, possibly break relations with the Taliban.
Mahmud assured Armitage that Pakistan was with the US in the fight against terrorism.
Cable instructs Ambassador to double-track the message with President Musharraf; Powell hoped to call Musharraf within hours.

key_claims: The US demanded Pakistan stop al-Qa'ida operatives at its border, intercept arms shipments and end logistical support for bin Ladin.
The US asked Pakistan to cut off fuel shipments and recruits/volunteers going to the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The US asked for blanket overflight, landing rights and access to Pakistani ports, airbases and border locations.
If evidence implicated bin Ladin and the Taliban kept harboring him, Pakistan was asked to break diplomatic relations with the Taliban and end support for it.
ISI chief Mahmud Ahmed assured Armitage that Pakistan was with the US, but the US sought an official response from Musharraf.
